limitations: Static, tool-free review. I executed nothing and claim no test results. The report's counts (145 prior cases, 166 final, 15 RED to 0, 153 denials preserved against original main, 57 production matrix, 15 bypass) were not re-run. The 145+3+2+15+1=166 arithmetic and the 5 operators x 3 separators=15 loop do reconcile with the supplied test file.

I traced the awk tokenizer by hand against GNU bash lexing. Real behavior may vary across awk implementations (BWK on macOS, mawk, gawk). I expect `[ \t;]` and `[@!?+*]` inside bracket expressions to work in all of them, but I did not check. I also did not check how the Bash tool delivers VT/FF/CR bytes. Claude Code may run commands under zsh, and I did not analyse zsh comment or extended-glob rules. Removing `(` from the comment set also leaves zsh `(#i)`-style constructs on the scanning, conservative side.

Fail-closed trade-off, not a defect: `#` after `|`, `&`, `(` or `)` is a real comment in bash, but the scanner no longer stops there. A genuine comment in that position that contains an odd quote or backtick will leave the scanner in an open-quote or open-tick state and push the input to the original raw-regex fallback. This only means extra false positives that match baseline behavior. Any quote or tick opened by such a comment either shows up as a payload, which is denied on network tokens, or leaves ambiguity set at END.

Any unquoted `@(`, `!(`, `?(`, `+(` or `*(` now selects the raw fallback regardless of whether extglob is enabled. This is a deliberate, documented over-approximation and returns those inputs to baseline behavior.

The guard remains a regex and heuristic tokenizer, not a shell parser or sandbox. Optional broader redesign: replace the awk tokenizer with a real shell parser, or deny any backtick substitution whose payload cannot be parsed. This is outside the scope of this repair.
The new per-character regex test costs little and is bounded by the existing 32768-character parser cap. I make no global latency claim. Large-input baseline latency is documented as pre-existing.

Cosmetic only: REPORT.md has missing spaces in places, for example 'base90cafd05...' and 'original91839087'. This does not affect source behavior. Other security and evidence scope, and the unchanged TDD source, are taken from the brief as previously passed and were not re-reviewed.
review_summary:
Static review of the T129 comment-boundary correction in `.claude/hooks/pre-bash-guard.sh`, checked against the original baseline and the changed tests. I found no concrete defects.

The prior HIGH is closed. A `#` now starts a comment only at line start or after a space, tab or `;`, so VT, FF, CR, `)`, `|`, `&` and `(` before `#` no longer hide a later live backtick substitution. For VT/FF/CR the scan continues and captures the `curl` payload. For the extglob forms (`@(a)#x`, `@(a|#b)`), the scan continues and the new unquoted extglob condition also sets `ambiguous=1`.

The new extglob condition covers the same class. It applies only when `quote==""`, and any of `@ ! ? + *` followed by `(` selects the original raw fallback instead of parsing patterns. This closes the apparent-boundary cases inside a pattern: space, tab and `;` before `#`. Each of those would otherwise have been mistaken for a comment start. The fallback regex matches the whitespace-squeezed command, so the tests' `shopt -s extglob` newline form is denied.

I also traced several things that could leave a gap, and they hold:
- A real comment that contains a quote or tick leaves the scanner open-quoted at END, so ambiguity is set and the input fails closed.
- Comment-hidden quote state carried into later lines either yields a payload that is denied on network tokens, or sets ambiguity.
- Single-quoted extglob prose is not flagged, because the check is gated on `quote==""` and quoted spans `continue` before it. The `quoted-extglob-prose` pass test is therefore consistent with the implementation.

The changed tests are well formed. Each new case would have been RED against the previous classes, and the loop's `check deny` expectations match the code paths. The control-character cases pass bytes through `jq --arg` and `$'...'` correctly. The one pass control is consistent with the single-quote path. Diffs against baseline show no relaxation of any deny path. All new behavior either denies or reverts to baseline fallback behavior. Verdict: pass, with no findings.
